t.7.49.1: But having seen Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, brought into the hermitage, Lakṣmaṇa, his mind dejected, felt terrible anguish.
t.7.49.2: And the greatly radiant one said to Sumantra, the counsellor-charioteer: "Behold the sorrow of the wise Rāma, born of his anguish over Sītā."
t.7.49.3: What could be more sorrowful for Rāghava than this, having abandoned his wife, the daughter of Janaka, whose conduct was pure?
t.7.49.4: O charioteer, I clearly think that Rāghava's separation from Vaidehī has come about through fate, for fate is hard to overcome.
t.7.49.5: For Rāghava, who in his wrath could slay the gods together with the Gandharvas, and the Asuras along with the Rākṣasas, even he submits to fate.
t.7.49.6: Formerly, at my father's command, I dwelt in Daṇḍaka, in that lonely and exceedingly dreadful forest, for nine years and five more.
t.7.49.7: More grievous still than that is the banishment of Sītā; because it was done on hearing the words of the townspeople, it seems cruel to me.
t.7.49.8: What ground in dharma, O sūta, has been found by the citizens, speakers of baseless words, in this fame-destroying deed concerning Maithilī?
t.7.49.9: Having heard these many and varied words spoken by Lakṣmaṇa, Sumantra joined his palms in reverence and spoke these words.
t.7.49.10: You should not grieve over Maithilī, O Saumitri. This was foreseen long ago by the brahmins in the presence of your father, O Lakṣmaṇa.
t.7.49.11: Rāma will surely be one whose lot is mostly sorrow, with but little happiness. In the course of a long time, that great and righteous-souled one will abandon you, and Maithilī too, and Śatrughna and Bharata as well.
t.7.49.12: But this was not to be told to you, O Saumitri, nor even to Bharata: the words that Durvāsas spoke, which the king never disclosed to any of you.
t.7.49.13: O bull among men, these words were spoken by the sage in the presence of the great king and of me as well, and in the presence of Vasiṣṭha.
t.7.49.14: Having heard the words of the sage, that bull among men said to me: “O Sūta, you must never speak of this anywhere in the presence of people.”
t.7.49.15: Being fully intent upon that word of that protector of the world, I would never make it false. Such is my resolve, O gentle one.
t.7.49.16: Gentle one, there is nothing at all that I may not tell you in your presence. If you wish to hear it, then listen, O Raghunandana.
t.7.49.17: Although I was once told a secret by the king, I shall nevertheless relate it, for fate is indeed hard to overcome.
t.7.49.18: Having heard that great speech of his, profound in meaning and in words, Saumitri then spoke these words to the charioteer: "Tell me the truth."
